# Kidneys

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Basics of nephrology > Kidneys*

[Original Article Link](/library/m60VlS)

---

## Summary

The kidneys are paired <u>retroperitoneal organs</u> located on either side of the <u>vertebral column</u> extending between the 12<sup>th</sup> thoracic and the 3<sup>rd</sup> lumbar <u>vertebral</u> levels. They play an important role in the excretion of waste products, the regulation of <u>extracellular fluid</u> volume and <u>osmolality</u>, the maintenance of acid-base balance, <u>hormone</u> synthesis (e.g., <u>erythropoietin</u>), and <u>gluconeogenesis</u>. The kidneys receive their blood supply from the paired <u>renal arteries</u> and drain into the paired <u>renal veins</u>. The <u>lymphatics</u> drain into the <u>paraaortic lymph nodes</u>. The left <u>renal vein</u> passes between the <u>abdominal aorta</u> and the <u>superior mesenteric artery</u>. The kidneys receive <u>sympathetic</u> innervation via the <u>sympathetic trunk</u> and <u>parasympathetic</u> innervation via the <u>vagus nerve</u>. Anatomically, the kidneys are composed of the <u>renal capsule</u>, <u>renal cortex</u>, <u>renal medulla</u>, <u>renal sinus</u>, and <u>renal hilum</u>. The <u>nephron</u> is the functional unit of the kidney, and it is composed of a <u>renal corpuscle</u> and a renal tubule. The <u>renal corpuscle</u> consists of the <u>glomerulus</u> and the <u>Bowman capsule</u>, which are separated by the <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> (<u>GFB</u>). The <u>GFB</u>, which is composed of the <u>fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium</u>, the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>, and the <u>podocyte</u> layer, is responsible for filtering blood plasma. The filtrate passes through the renal tubule, which is divided into the <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u>, the <u>loop of Henle</u>, the <u>distal convoluted tubule</u>, and the <u>collecting duct</u>. In the renal tubule, urine is formed from the filtrate via reabsorption, secretion, and excretion of substances. The kidneys originate embryologically from the <u>mesoderm</u>.

## Gross anatomy

### Overview




* Characteristics

* Reddish-brown, bean-shaped, paired <u>retroperitoneal organs</u> lying on either side of the <u>vertebral column</u> at the level of T12–L3

* Each kidney weighs approximately 5 oz–6.3 oz

* Dimensions: 10–12 cm in length, 4–6 cm in width, and 3–4 cm in anteroposterior dimension

* Relations

* Located at the superior pole: <u>adrenal gland</u> (within the <u>perirenal fat</u>)

* Anteriorly

* Left kidney: <u>spleen</u>, <u>stomach</u>, <u>pancreas</u>, <u>splenic flexure</u>, <u>jejunum</u>

* Right kidney: right lobe of the <u>liver</u>, descending <u>duodenum</u>, hepatic flexure

* Posteriorly

* Both kidneys: <u>diaphragm</u>, <u>psoas major</u>, <u>quadratus lumborum</u>, the subcostal, <u>iliohypogastric nerve</u>, <u>ilioinguinal nerve</u>

* Left kidney: 11<sup>th</sup> and 12<sup>th</sup><u>ribs</u>

* Right kidney: 12<sup>th</sup><u>rib</u>

### Internal macrostructure




* Renal cortex

* The outermost layer of the renal <u>parenchyma</u> (∼ 10 mm thick)

* Surrounds the <u>renal medulla</u> and extends inwards (as renal columns) dividing the medulla into <u>renal pyramids</u>

* Contains the <u>glomeruli</u>, <u>proximal convoluted tubules</u>, <u>distal convoluted tubules</u>, and cortical <u>collecting ducts</u>

* Renal medulla

* Consists of several renal medullary pyramids separated by the renal columns

* The base of each pyramid faces the outer cortex, the apex faces the <u>renal sinus</u> and forms a renal papilla, which drains into a minor calyx.

* Contains the loops of Henle and <u>collecting ducts</u>, which merge to form the <u>papillary</u> ducts at the <u>renal papillae</u>

* Blood flow in the <u>renal medulla</u> is relatively low compared to that in the <u>renal cortex</u>. [[1]](/library/Rpbl6u)

* Facilitates the development of an <u>osmolality</u> gradient that allows for effective <u>urine concentration</u>

* Causes medullary vulnerability to <u>hypoxia</u> when <u>renal blood flow</u> is decreased (renal <u>ischemia</u>)

* Renal sinus

* The inner portion of the kidney containing the renal calyces and <u>renal pelvis</u>

* The minor calyces draining from each <u>renal papilla</u> merge to form major calyces.

* The major calyces merge to form the renal pelvis, which represents the <u>proximal</u> portion of the <u>ureter</u>.

* Renal hilum: The <u>medial</u> <u>fissure</u> on each kidney where the <u>renal pelvis</u>, vessels, and nerves enter and exit

> [!NOTE]
> The kidneys receive 20–25% of the <u>cardiac output</u>. Despite this, the medulla is relatively <u>hypoxic</u> and vulnerable to <u>ischemic</u> damage.




### Surrounding structures




Each kidney is encapsulated by layers of <u>fascia</u> and fat. These layers comprise (from the outside to the inside):




* Pararenal fat: the <u>adipose tissue</u> <u>superficial</u> to the renal <u>fascia</u>; protects the kidneys from trauma

* <u>Perirenal fascia</u> 

* Definition: a single multilaminated <u>connective tissue</u> structure that envelops each kidney and <u>adrenal gland</u> along with a layer of <u>perirenal fat</u>

* Divisions

* <u>Anterior</u> <u>perirenal fascia</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> <u>perirenal fascia</u>

* Anatomical boundaries

* <u>Anterior</u>: The <u>anterior</u> <u>perirenal fascia</u> extends in front of the renal vessels and allows for communication between <u>perirenal spaces</u>.

* <u>Posterior</u>: The <u>posterior</u> <u>perirenal fascia</u> fuses with the <u>fascia</u> of <u>psoas major</u>.

* Superior: The superior <u>perirenal space</u> opens to the upper abdominal extraperitoneal space in continuity with the <u>bare area of the liver</u>.

* <u>Lateral</u>: The <u>anterior</u> <u>perirenal fascia</u> fuses with the <u>coronary ligament</u> (on the right) and <u>gastrosplenic ligament</u> (on the left).

* Inferior: The <u>fascia</u> surrounds the <u>ureter</u> and fuses with the iliac <u>fascia</u>.

* Perirenal fat: the <u>adipose tissue</u> that envelopes the kidneys; covered by renal <u>fascia</u>

* Renal capsule: a thin layer of <u>collagen</u>-rich <u>connective tissue</u> that forms a fibrous capsule around the kidney and <u>adrenal gland</u>





### Vasculature, <u>lymphatics</u>, and innervation




|  | <br>Description <br> |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Arteries</u> | <br><br>* The right and left <u>renal arteries</u> branch laterally from the aorta at the level of L1–2, just inferior to the <u>superior mesenteric artery</u>, and enter the kidney at the hilum.<br><br>* Accessory <u>renal arteries</u> are present in 30% of individuals, they also branch laterally from the aorta and enter at the hilum.<br><br>* The <u>renal arteries</u> give off branches to the <u>adrenal gland</u> (<u>inferior suprarenal artery</u>) and <u>ureter</u>.<br><br>* <u>Renal blood flow</u>: <u>renal artery</u> → <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> branches → segmental <u>arteries</u> → lobar <u>arteries</u> → interlobar <u>arteries</u> → arcuate <u>arteries</u> → interlobular <u>arteries</u> → <u>afferent arteriole</u> → <u>glomerulus</u> → <u>efferent arteriole</u> → vasa recta (→ venous system)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Veins</u> | <br><br>* A single <u>vein</u> exits each kidney at the hilum <u>anterior</u> to the <u>renal artery</u> and drains into the vena cava.<br><br>* The left <u>renal vein</u> is longer than the right <u>renal vein</u> because it runs a longer course to the <u>inferior vena cava</u>, which is situated on the right side of the body.<br><br>* The left <u>renal vein</u> crosses the midline between the aorta  and the <u>superior mesenteric artery</u> (SMA).<br><br>* The left suprarenal and <u>gonadal veins</u> drain into the left <u>renal vein</u>, whereas on the right, they drain directly into the vena cava.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lymphatics</u> | <br>* Drain into the <u>paraaortic lymph nodes</u><br><br> |
| <u>Sympathetic</u> innervation | <br>* <u>Sympathetic trunk</u> → <u>renal plexus</u> surrounding each <u>renal artery</u><br><br> |
| <u>Parasympathetic</u> innervation | <br>* None  [[2]](/library/3mYS2p)[[3]](/library/ES08Yf)<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The left <u>renal vein</u> drains blood from the left kidney, the <u>left suprarenal vein</u>, and the <u>left gonadal vein</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Blood Arrives through the Afferent <u>arteriole</u> and blood Exits through the Efferent <u>arterioles</u>.

## Microscopic anatomy

### Nephron




* Description

* The functional unit of the kidney, composed of a <u>renal corpuscle</u> and a renal tubule

* There are approx. 1 million <u>nephrons</u> per kidney  [[4]](/library/nJb7uu)

* Function

* The <u>renal corpuscle</u> filters fluid from the blood, producing an ultrafiltrate

* The renal tubule resorbs and secretes substances from the ultrafiltrate, producing urine

* See ”<u>Physiology of the kidney</u>.”

* Two types of <u>nephrons</u>: cortical and juxtamedullary

* Distinguished by the location of the <u>glomerulus</u>

* Cortical <u>nephrons</u> (approx. 85%)

* Located close to the outer part of the <u>renal cortex</u>

* Short <u>loop of Henle</u>

* Mainly regulatory and excretory functions

* Juxtamedullary <u>nephrons</u> (approx. 15%)

* <u>Glomerulus</u> near the junction of the <u>renal cortex</u> and medulla

* Long <u>loop of Henle</u>

* Main function: concentration or dilution of urine





![Microstructure of the kidney](media/ap9203ijrvv8eijz3r1fgntp.jpg)

Microstructure of the kidney




#### Renal corpuscle




* Description

* Located in the <u>renal cortex</u>

* Formed of a tuft of <u>capillaries</u> (the <u>glomerulus</u>) enclosed by the <u>Bowman capsule</u>

* The <u>glomerulus</u> forms the vascular pole of the corpuscle

* The <u>Bowman capsule</u> forms the urinary pole of the corpuscle

* Within the <u>Bowman capsule</u> is the Bowman space, which is continuous with the renal tubule

* The <u>Bowman capsule</u> is separated from the <u>capillaries</u> of the <u>glomerulus</u> by the <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u>

* Components

* Glomerulus: a tuft of <u>capillaries</u> within the <u>Bowman capsule</u> formed of three parts

* Afferent arterioles: the blood vessel that enters and supplies the <u>glomerulus</u> of the kidney for filtration

* Branch into <u>anastomosing</u> <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillaries</u>, between <u>capillaries</u>, lie intraglomerular mesangial cells (contractile cells capable of <u>phagocytosis</u> and <u>lysosomal</u> degradation)

* Efferent arterioles: the blood vessel that carries previously filtered blood away from the <u>glomerulus</u> (drains from the <u>glomerulus</u>)

* Bowman capsule: cup-like sac that surrounds the <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillaries</u>

* Outer (parietal) surface: simple <u>squamous epithelium</u>

* Inner (<u>visceral</u>) surface: <u>podocytes</u>

* The space between the parietal and <u>visceral</u> surfaces, which is continuous with the <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u>, is referred to as the Bowman space.

* Function: filtration of blood across the glomerular filtration barrier, forming ultrafiltrate within the Bowman space

* The <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> separates the blood within the <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillaries</u> from the ultrafiltrate in the Bowman space.

* Water, <u>electrolytes</u>, and other small molecules cross the filtration barrier to form the ultrafiltrate.

* Cells and large or negatively-charged molecules, e.g., <u>proteins</u>, cannot cross the filtration barrier and remain within the blood (size and charge selectivity).

* The <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> is composed of three layers: the <u>fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium</u>, the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>, and the <u>podocyte</u> layer.





| Layers of the <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Layer | Description | Clinical relevance | Function |  |
| Size barrier | Charge barrier |  |  |  |
| Fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium | <br>* Porous <u>capillary</u> <u>endothelium</u> (fenestrated <u>endothelium</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Preeclampsia</u><br><br> | <br>* Molecules > 100–50 nm<br><br> | <br>* Negatively charged glycoproteins (e.g., with <u>heparan sulfate</u> on the <u>GBM</u>) prevent the entry of negatively charged molecules (e.g., <u>albumin</u>).<br><br> |
| <br>Glomerular basement membrane (<u>GBM</u>) | <br>* Consists of 3 layers <br><br>* <u>Lamina rara</u> interna: covers the <u>endothelium</u> and contains <u>heparan sulfate</u><br><br>* <u>Lamina densa</u>: consists of <u>type IV collagen</u> and <u>laminin</u><br><br>* <u>Lamina rara</u> <u>externa</u>: covers <u>podocytes</u> and contains <u>heparan sulfate</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Goodpasture syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Alport syndrome</u><br><br>* Diabetic <u>glomerulosclerosis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Molecules > 70 nm<br><br> |  |
| Podocytes | <br><br>* Form the <u>visceral</u> <u>epithelial</u> layer of the <u>Bowman capsule</u><br><br>* Foot processes surround the <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillaries</u> and leave filtration slits (slit diaphragms)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Minimal change disease</u><br><br> | <br>* Molecules > 50–60 nm<br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> ensures that large and/or negatively charged molecules in the blood cannot pass into the <u>Bowman capsule</u>.

#### Renal tubules




| Overview of the renal tubules |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Segments |  | Location | Microscopy | Function |
| <br>Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) |  | <br>* <u>Renal cortex</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Tall, cuboidal cells with brush border (long apical <u>microvilli</u>)<br><br>* Basal invaginations with multiple <u>mitochondria</u><br><br>* Contains <u>lysosomes</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Each segment has a distinct <u>epithelial</u> lining and function<br><br>* Receive the ultrafiltrate from the <u>renal corpuscle</u><br><br>* Transport and concentrates the ultrafiltrate<br><br>* Form urine via reabsorption, secretion, and excretion of substances<br><br>* See ”<u>Physiology of the kidney</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| Loop of Henle | Thin descending loop of Henle | <br>* <u>Renal medulla</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Smaller diameter than PCT<br><br>* Flat, <u>squamous epithelium</u> (resembles <u>capillary</u> <u>endothelium</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| Thick ascending loop of Henle | <br><br>* Wider diameter than the descending segment<br><br>* <u>Epithelium</u> with variable short brush border and <u>tight junctions</u> (impermeable to water)<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| Distal convoluted tubule |  | <br>* <u>Renal cortex</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Directly adjacent to the <u>nephron</u>'s <u>glomerulus</u><br><br>* <u>Squamous epithelium</u> of variable thickness with short brush border and <u>tight junctions</u> (impermeable to water)<br><br><br> |  |
| Connecting tubule and collecting duct |  | <br>* <u>Renal cortex</u> and <u>renal medulla</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Connecting tubule</u> collects urine from several <u>nephrons</u><br><br>* Cuboidal or <u>columnar epithelium</u><br><br>* <u>Principal cells</u> with <u>tight junctions</u> (with <u>aldosterone</u> <u>receptors</u>)<br><br>* α-Intercalated cells and β-intercalated cells with <u>tight junctions</u><br><br><br> |  |





![Structure of renal parenchyma](media/d9bmo6niqbxi3w57qxktrcps.jpg)

Structure of renal parenchyma




### Juxtaglomerular complex




* Definition

* A specialized structure within the <u>nephron</u>

* Located between the <u>distal convoluted tubule</u> (<u>DCT</u>) and the <u>afferent arteriole</u> of the <u>nephron</u>

* Maintains the <u>GFR</u> by regulating the <u>renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system</u> (<u>RAAS</u>)

* Components 

* Juxtaglomerular cells

* Modified <u>smooth muscle cells</u> located in the <u>afferent arterioles</u>

* Function: <u>renin</u> synthesis

* Macula densa 

* Composed of tall cuboidal cells located at the <u>distal</u> end of the thick <u>ascending loop of Henle</u>

* Monitors the NaCl concentration within the lumen of the <u>DCT</u>

* Hypoosmolar urine;   triggers the release of <u>renin</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u> of the <u>efferent arteriole</u> → increase in <u>GFR</u>

* Hyperosmolar urine;   triggers the release of <u>adenosine</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u> of the <u>afferent arteriole</u> → decrease in <u>GFR</u>

* Extraglomerular mesangial cells [[3]](/library/ES08Yf)

* Play a role in autoregulation of blood flow to the kidney (exact functioning is not entirely understood)

* Form a network of cells, connecting the sensory cells of the <u>macula densa</u> with juxtaglomerular effector cells

* May also signal to contractile <u>glomerular</u> mesangial cells and, thereby, directly affect <u>vasoconstriction</u>

## Function

* Production of urine

* Excretion of metabolic waste and end-products of metabolism (e.g., <u>urea</u>, drugs)

* Regulation of <u>extracellular fluid</u> volume and <u>osmolality</u>

* Maintenance of acid-base balance

* Maintenance of <u>electrolyte</u> concentrations

* Regulation of blood pressure and blood volume

* Participation in <u>gluconeogenesis</u> (<u>glutamine</u> and <u>glutamate</u>) and <u>ketogenesis</u>

* <u>Hormone</u> synthesis

* <u>Erythropoietin</u>

* <u>Calciferol</u>

* <u>Prostaglandins</u>

* <u>Dopamine</u>

* <u>Renin</u>

* See also “<u>Physiology of the kidney</u>.”

## Embryology

### General




* Origin: <u>intermediate mesoderm</u>

* Development begins at the 4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>.

* Precursor cells migrate <u>cranial</u> to <u>caudal</u>.

* The <u>urogenital ridge</u> gives rise to the <u>pronephros</u>, <u>mesonephros</u>, and <u>metanephros</u>.





### Stages   [[5]](/library/zuXrF-)



1. * Pronephros: the first embryonic excretory organ (rudimentary in human embryos)

* Arises in the cervical region of the embryo during the 3<sup>rd</sup>–4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>

* Migrates <u>caudally</u> to connect with the pronephric duct

* Composed of nephrotomes and nephric tubules → temporary excretory function

* Degenerates with the development of the <u>mesonephros</u>
2. * Mesonephros: the second embryonic excretory organ, developing <u>caudally</u> to the <u>pronephros</u> and degenerating with the development of the <u>metanephros</u>

* Arises in the 4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>

* <u>Cranial</u> end: functions as interim kidney during the <u>1<sup>st</sup> trimester</u>

* Forms <u>Bowman capsule</u>

* Functions until the end of the 2<sup>nd</sup> month before it degenerates

* <u>Caudal</u> end: contributes to male genital system

* Mesonephric tubules contribute to the <u>mesonephric duct</u>.

* The <u>mesonephric duct</u> forms the <u>epididymis</u>, <u>ductus deferens</u>, <u>seminal vesicle</u>, and the <u>ejaculatory duct</u> in male embryos.
3. * Metanephros: the third embryonic excretory organ, developing <u>caudally</u> to the <u>mesonephros</u> and persisting as the permanent kidney

* Arises during the 5<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>

* Canalization is complete by the 10<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>.

* Maturing of the kidneys continues until week 35–36 of <u>embryonic development</u>.

* Components

* Ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum)

* Originates from the <u>caudal</u> end of the <u>mesonephric duct</u>

* Differentiates into the <u>collecting duct</u> system: <u>ureter</u>, <u>renal pelvis</u>, major calyces, minor calyces, and <u>collecting ducts</u>

* Ureteropelvic junction: junction between <u>ureter</u> and <u>renal pelvis</u>

* Canalizes last and represents the most common site of prenatal <u>urinary tract obstruction</u>

* Obstruction of the <u>ureteropelvic junction</u> may cause prenatal <u>hydronephrosis</u>, which can be discovered during <u>prenatal ultrasound</u> screenings.

* Metanephric blastema (<u>metanephric mesenchyme</u>)

* Differentiation stimulated by <u>ureteric bud</u> signals

* Differentiates into <u>nephrons</u>: <u>glomerulus</u>, <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u>, <u>loop of Henle</u>, and <u>distal convoluted tubule</u>

* <u>Congenital anomalies of the kidneys</u> can result from, e.g., due to abnormal interaction between the <u>ureteric bud</u> and the metanephritic <u>blastema</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>ureteropelvic junction</u> canalizes last and is the most common site of obstruction.




> [!NOTE]
> If the inferior poles of both kidneys fuse during <u>fetal development</u>, they form a <u>horseshoe kidney</u> and become trapped underneath the <u>inferior mesenteric artery</u>.

## Clinical significance

* <u>Congenital anomalies of the kidneys</u>

* <u>Renal cyst</u> disorders

* <u>Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease</u>

* Simple <u>renal cysts</u> and complex <u>renal cysts</u>

* <u>Acute kidney injury</u>

* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u>

* <u>Glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Tubulointerstitial nephritis</u>

* <u>Renal tubular acidosis</u>

* <u>Nephrolithiasis</u>

* <u>Nephrotic syndrome</u>

* <u>Nephritic syndrome</u>
